about: Legato 45-second response prompts (coach-written, text only, passage-agnostic). The first seven ids keep the exact text of legato.RESPONSE_PROMPTS so existing sessions back-fill to an id. level follows the legato flow level (1 one move, 2 two-part, 3 constraint or audience switch). Selection: no prompt within the last 14 legato sessions, no type twice in a row, level = today's flow level when available.

prompts.text: In your own words: what is the author asking of the reader?
Agree or disagree with the author. One reason, one example.
Retell the passage to a colleague who has not read it.
Where would this idea help you at work this week?
What would you say back to the author?
Describe a moment from your own life this passage reminds you of.
Give the passage's message in three sentences, then one question it raises.
Sum up the passage in one sentence, then say why it matters.
Name the author's main point, then the line that best supports it.
Give the message in exactly two sentences: the claim, then the reason.
Say the author's point three ways: one word, one sentence, one example.
Which sentence in the passage do you agree with most, and why?
Which line do you push back on? Say why, then what you would say instead.
Argue the author is right for 20 seconds, then wrong for 20 seconds.
Agree with the author, then name the one situation where this advice fails.
Name one habit this passage asks you to start tomorrow.
Which customer conversation this month would have gone better with this idea, and how?
Turn the passage into one rule for your team, and give the reason behind it.
Apply this to a project you are on: one risk it reveals, one action you will take.
Use this idea to rescue a meeting that is going badly. What do you say first?
Give the author's point as a one-breath headline for an executive.
In one sentence, tell a busy manager why this idea is worth a minute.
Headline first for a CFO: what this idea saves or costs, then offer detail.
Tell an account leader in two sentences why this idea matters to the customer.
A CTO gives you 30 seconds: headline, one proof point, one ask.
An executive says, 'This is old advice.' Answer with a headline, then one fact.
Who in your life would agree with this author? Say why.
Tell a 30-second story where you saw this idea work, or fail.
Describe someone who lives this passage. What do they do differently?
Tell a story from your work that proves the author wrong, then what you learned.
Retell the passage as a software project story: situation, choice, result.
What question would you ask the author if you could?
What is one thing the author leaves out?
Give the strongest objection to this passage, then answer it.
What would a sceptical engineer say about this, and how would you reply?
Steelman the opposite view for 20 seconds, then say where you land.
Find the hidden assumption in the passage and test it with an example.
Explain the passage to a ten-year-old in three sentences.
Explain this passage to a new engineer, with one example from tech.
Teach the idea as three steps someone could follow today.
Teach the idea to a sceptical customer without quoting the passage.
Give a 45-second mini-talk on this idea: hook, point, example, close.
